comment: My PulsePoint doesnt support the work described because the stakeholders I collaborate with arent located at my assigned PulsePoint. My work requires collaboration with partners who are distributed across multiple states. Reporting to my PulsePoint has not increased in-person collaboration. The employees in my department who support my work are either assigned to other PulsePoints or are not located near any PulsePoint, which means they continue to meet with me virtually while I am in the office. Over the past three years of this requirement, I have not been able to meet in person at my PulsePoint with the people I work with most closely, because we are assigned to different PulsePoints, work remotely in different locations, or have approved exceptions. As a result, the requirement does not add meaningful value to my role  my meetings and collaboration remain primarily virtual (video calls and conference calls) regardless of where I am physically located. I believe the PulsePoint model is most beneficial for departments where the majority of a direct team and key partners report to the same PulsePoint and can regularly collaborate in person. The current frequency requirement creates a significant financial burden. Due to my job grade, I am required to report three times per week. With current fuel costs, this adds approximately $250–$300 per month in gas alone, in addition to increased vehicle wear and maintenance (more frequent oil changes, higher mileage, and reduced vehicle value). The commute also adds substantial time, 30 to 60 minutes each day depending on traffic and accidents. Since some employees report fewer days or not at all, this also creates an uneven financial impact. If in-office attendance is required for certain roles, considering a form of offset such as a gas card, commuting stipend, or pay differential so the requirement wont disproportionately affect employees who must commute more frequently, particularly in the current economic environment

Conducting monthly one-on-one meetings often requires me to coordinate around my remote work schedule because I can frequently provide a more private setting at home than in the office. This creates additional scheduling challenges and can impact the effectiveness of those discussions. While the office design is visually appealing and promotes an open environment, I do not feel it fully supports the nature of the work many of us perform. The current neighborhood model can create significant distractions, as employees from very different departments and job functions are often seated in close proximity. As a result, it is common to hear lengthy conversations or calls that are unrelated to my work, making it difficult to maintain focus throughout the day. In the previous office configuration, workspaces were more intentionally aligned with job functions. For example, call center teams, managers, and business teams were generally located in separate areas, which helped balance collaboration needs with concentration and noise management. The combination of higher cubicle walls and white-noise systems also provided a greater sense of privacy and reduced distractions. While the designated quiet zones are a valuable resource, they are not always a practical solution for employees who have a mix of focused work and meetings throughout the day. Frequently relocating between workspaces can be disruptive and reduce productivity. I would encourage consideration of additional privacy and noise-reduction measures, such as higher workstation partitions, expanded sound-masking solutions, more dedicated spaces for confidential conversations, or a reassessment of neighborhood assignments based on work type. These changes could help create an environment that better supports both collaboration and focused, productive work.

One area that could be better supported is focused individual work that requires sustained concentration. The shared workspace model, while beneficial for flexibility, can introduce distractions due to the open-office environment, background conversations, and the lack of a dedicated workspace. Re-establishing a workstation each visit and working from a non-personalized space can reduce efficiency compared to an environment that is consistently configured to support an individual's work style. For my role, much of my work involves technical analysis, documentation development, assessment reviews, policy interpretation, and research activities that benefit from a controlled and distraction-free environment. My home office is specifically configured to support these activities, including a dedicated workspace and technology setup that allows me to work more efficiently. Additionally, because my team and key stakeholders are distributed across multiple geographic locations, most collaboration occurs through Microsoft Teams regardless of whether I am working from home or from a PulsePoint location. As a result, the in-office experience often consists of participating in the same virtual meetings that would occur remotely, while also managing the additional distractions associated with a shared workspace. While PulsePoints support scheduled meetings and provide a location for in-person interaction when needed, I believe there is an opportunity to further improve support for focused technical work and employees whose collaboration primarily occurs with geographically dispersed teams.

Several aspects of the office environment create challenges that impact productivity and the ability to effectively support associates. The most significant barrier is background noise. As a frontline manager, I spend much of my day on calls, coaching team members, and handling sensitive conversations. Associates often comment that they can hear surrounding conversations more clearly than they can hear me. The lower cubicle walls provide limited sound buffering, making it difficult to maintain a professional call environment. The office temperature is also consistently very cold, which can be distracting and uncomfortable throughout the day. In addition, limited access to standing desks and uncomfortable office chairs can contribute to physical discomfort during extended periods of work. Compared to the previous office setup, the higher cubicle walls provided greater privacy and reduced noise distractions, making it easier to perform daily responsibilities effectively while onsite. The current limitation of one private room reservation per day for up to two hours can also be challenging for frontline leaders who regularly conduct coaching sessions, confidential discussions, and associate meetings. Increased flexibility for private workspace reservations would better support productivity and allow for more effective time spent in the office. It may be helpful for those involved in workspace planning to observe a frontline manager's typical workday to better understand these challenges and identify solutions that support both leaders and associates.

Air Quality and Temperature at PulsePoint Air quality at PulsePoint is extremely poor and is causing frequent respiratory irritation. Even employees without allergies report coughing and sneezing  many, including myself and my team, take allergy medication before arriving. Although we’ve confirmed filters are changed regularly, an underlying air quality issue persists—particularly when the HVAC system is running (most notably in winter). Temperature control is also inconsistent across floors. While the first floor is generally comfortable, the second floor is often excessively hot in the mornings, with air conditioning not engaging until the afternoon. In mild morning conditions (e.g., 65–68°F even when the afternoon forecast reaches ~80°F in Woodland Hills), the heating system runs until midday before switching to A/C. This creates an uncomfortable environment, especially for executives in suits. A cooler baseline would be preferable, since layers can be added if needed, whereas overheating (mid-to-high 70s indoors) is difficult to manage. A target range of 69–71°F (up to 73°F) aligns with typical office standards. Also, more small conference rooms and work capsules are needed to support heavy on-site meeting and call demands. Directors are on-site three days per week and are in calls most of the day, which can still be disruptive in open areas. Leaders need capsules (not phone booths) and small rooms for 2+ hours daily for team and cross-functional collaboration. Supporting the Health Plan President is challenging due to limited offices with tables/chairs - only 255-B corner office has this setup - it would be nice to add it to all Staff VP offices. Large CA Health Plan meetings (3/month, 14–25 attendees) often face space constraints  more large-room options are needed beyond the single 1st-floor room.

Indy's PulsePoint offers great amenities overall, and I appreciate the investment that has been made in creating the space. One challenge, however, is that the in-office experience is very different depending on whether you have access to a dedicated office or closer parking options. For most of us, much of the day is spent in virtual meetings. Since offices below staff vp level can only be reserved same day and for two-hour increments, it is difficult to plan ahead for days that require extensive calls, collaboration, or focused work. Working from the open cubicle space is challenging due to the level of activity and noise and often requires wearing a headset continuously throughout the day. After many consecutive hours of meetings, wearing either over-ear or in-ear headsets is physically uncomfortable. While phone booths can help with noise and privacy, they are not a practical alternative for extended work because workspace and monitor options are limited. Many meetings require multiple screens, which means associates need to bring and set up their own second monitor if they plan to work from a phone booth. In addition, on days with back-to-back meetings, finding an available phone booth between calls can be difficult and can result in being late to meetings while searching for an open space. The walk from the parking garage to the building also adds a meaningful amount of time to the commute. On lower-utilization office days, it would be helpful to explore opportunities for closer parking access from both a safety and time-management perspective. Additional flexibility around workspace reservations and parking would help make time in the office more productive and effective. I appreciate this survey as a way to share feedback!

I have gotten kicked out of it several times due to carrying something or my backpack sets it off. If there were ever a situation in the parking area that I needed to get into this building quickly, such as a shooter, we would never be able to quickly get multiple people in the door quickly. The other side of the building where security sits does not have one. It has a normal door. No one comes in that way because the parking lot is on the side with the revolving door. I have been told that security has an override for the revolving door if an emergency occurs. Unfortunately, they can't even see that door from where they sit. It would not be a timely reaction to ensure that occurred.  If you park in the parking lot and swipe to come into the building through the revolving door and you have a meeting in one of the conference rooms across from security, you have to swipe back out of the building to get to them. So essentially it looks like you swiped into work and immediately swiped back out. Also, the supposed purpose of the swiping in and out is to account for our safety in case of an emergency. If the roster that security would have at the time of the emergency shows me swiped out, how will they know to account for me. It just doesn't make sense.  Unfortunately, in today's world these are the things that we need to think about. comment: Pulse point is well maintained and supported by good staff. very inviting for associates to come to office to work.

I do not feel that the current workspace design fully supports the needs of my role as a frontline manager. A significant part of my job involves coaching, mentoring, conducting one-on-one meetings, and having confidential conversations with associates. To effectively perform these responsibilities, I would benefit from a dedicated workstation with greater privacy, such as higher cubicle walls or designated manager workspaces that better accommodate sensitive discussions and focused work. I would also like to share feedback regarding the current hybrid work requirements. While I understand the organization's goals in increasing in-office presence, my experience has been that I was more productive and maintained a better work-life balance when working remotely the majority of the time and coming into the office one day per week. The flexibility of that arrangement allowed me to incorporate healthy habits, such as taking a walk during lunch breaks, which improved my focus, energy level, and overall well-being. The current requirement to commute to the office three days per week has reduced that flexibility and added additional strain. Because my entire team works remotely, my in-office presence does not significantly increase collaboration with my direct reports, and I often find that I can perform my responsibilities more effectively from my home office environment. Additionally, the increased in-office requirement has created challenges for my family. My wife and I care for our non-verbal son with special needs, and the additional commute time and reduced flexibility can add stress to an already demanding caregiving schedule. While I fully understand that workplace decisions must balance many factors and cannot be based solely on individual circumstances, I wanted to share how these requirements have affected my personal and professional experience. Overall, I am proud to work for Elevance Health and appreciate the company's willingness to seek employee feedback.

My feedback is less about the facility itself and more about my specific work model. As a director, I manage a team that is distributed across the country and offshore, with no direct reports based in Indianapolis. Because of that, I spend most of my day in virtual meetings regardless of whether I am working from home or from the office. When I come into the office, my experience is largely the same as it is at home: I connect my laptop to monitors, put on a headset, and participate in virtual meetings throughout the day. One enhancement that could make the office more compelling for employees in similar roles would be the addition of individual collaboration rooms or dedicated virtual-work spaces designed for a single person. comment: My overall experience has been positive, and I appreciate the effort that has gone into creating a flexible and welcoming workplace. If there is one opportunity I would highlight, it is to think about the PulsePoint not only as a place where associates work, but as a place where community is built. Most associates can accomplish their individual work from many locations. The unique value of the PulsePoint is the opportunity to build relationships, trust, and connections that are difficult to create virtually. Today, many of us work alongside people we do not know because we are on different teams, and the physical space, services, and technology are often optimized for planned interactions rather than organic ones. The Community Managers and Connection Council are doing an excellent job creating structured opportunities for engagement. Building on that foundation, I believe the next evolution of the PulsePoint is to create more opportunities for associate-to-associate connection through shared experiences, community-focused spaces, and tools that help people discover common interests and activities. The strongest workplaces are not just places where work happens—they are places where relationships form, ideas spread, and a sense of belonging develops naturally.

comment: I believe the Pulse Point requirement should be reevaluated for teams that are fully distributed across the United States. My direct team and key collaborators are located across the United States, and there is not a single person in my local Pulse Point with whom I work or collaborate with. The intended benefit of in-person collaboration is not being realized. Instead, employees spend most of the day on back-to-back virtual meetings, often in shared office spaces that can be difficult to reserve and are not always conducive to productivity or comfort. Many legacy employees successfully worked remotely long before COVID, demonstrating that effective collaboration and performance can occur without a physical office presence. Additionally, the current policy is creating morale challenges. With numerous exceptions in place, employees who are required to come into the office often feel they are being treated inconsistently or unfairly. Rather than improving engagement, the requirement is having the opposite effect for many employees. Given the limited collaboration benefits for distributed teams, it may be worth reconsidering the requirement and evaluating whether reducing office footprint could provide meaningful cost savings while maintaining productivity and employee satisfaction.  Furthermore, the location of this Pulse Point presents additional challenges. Many employees perceive the surrounding area as poorly maintained and have concerns about personal safety, particularly when commuting early in the morning or after dark.

I recognize that this decision is likely outside of your direct control, and I appreciate your willingness to listen to employee feedback. That said, I wanted to share my perspective on the office attendance mandate. One of the values we consistently promote is work-life balance and providing employees with flexibility to manage both their professional and personal responsibilities effectively. Requiring employees to be in the office a set number of days each week feels somewhat at odds with that message, particularly when many teams have demonstrated that they can be highly productive and collaborative in a virtual environment. For roles like mine, where the majority of the day is spent in virtual meetings with colleagues located in different markets, the requirement to be physically present in the office does not necessarily enhance collaboration or productivity. Instead, it can create additional logistical challenges without a clear business benefit. I fully support opportunities for meaningful in-person connection and collaboration. However, a more flexible approach that considers the nature of individual roles and work responsibilities would seem more aligned with the culture of trust, flexibility, and work-life balance that we strive to promote.

comment: Overall, my PulsePoint experience is positive, and I appreciate the effort that has gone into creating an attractive, well-maintained, and functional workplace. The services, building operations, cleanliness, and workplace technology support have all been strong. The primary disconnect is between the design assumptions of the workspace and the realities of my role. My work consists largely of forecasting, data analysis, reporting, and collaboration with remote colleagues. For much of my tenure, I have had little to no in-person interaction with members of my immediate team, meaning most collaboration occurs through Teams regardless of location. As a result, commuting to the office often means performing the same virtual work I would perform elsewhere, but with a smaller workstation, fewer monitors, more ambient distractions, and less environmental control. For roles that depend on sustained concentration and extensive computer use, factors such as noise levels, workstation ergonomics, monitor configurations, and temperature have a greater impact on productivity than amenities or collaborative spaces. My feedback should not be interpreted as criticism of the facility itself. The PulsePoint is attractive, clean, well-operated, and easy to use. My responses reflect a desire to better align the workspace experience with the needs of employees whose work is primarily analytical, computer-based, and conducted with remote teams.

I want to emphasize that I support this effort and the intent behind PulsePoint—creating more opportunities for in-person collaboration. However, I’m finding it difficult to realize that benefit in practice. Effective in-person collaboration is limited when immediate teams and key partner teams are not co-located at the same PulsePoint. In my case, only 3 of the 11 people on my team are required to go into an office, and none of the three of us are assigned to the same PulsePoint. As a result, coming into the office often still means working virtually—just from a PulsePoint instead of from home. Additionally, the current setup can create productivity impacts. Each visit often requires time to re-establish a functional workspace (e.g., adjusting monitors/chairs, locating missing peripherals, resolving unplugged cords, or addressing monitor/equipment issues). That repeated “set up and troubleshoot” time, combined with a still-virtual working model, can reduce efficiency rather than improve it. If the goal is increased collaboration and productivity, I believe stronger co-location strategies (where possible) and more consistent workstation readiness would make a meaningful difference.
